πάντα συνεστη κέναι ἢ τὴν ἡδονὴν τέλος εἶναι τῶν ἀγαθῶν, καὶ τἆλλα λέγων ὅσα
τῆς ἔξω καὶ δοκούσης σοφίας ὕθλοι καὶ λῆροι τυγχάνουσιν· οὗτος γὰρ ἀληθῶς
μωρός ἐστιν καὶ ταῦτα τὰ δόγματα μωρία εἰσίν. καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς πᾶσαν Ἑλληνικὴν
καὶ βαρβαρικὴν ἐξετάζων φιλοσοφίαν ἐρεῖς ὅτι ἐν οἷς διαφωνεῖ πρὸς τὴν Χριστοῦ
διδασκαλίαν μωρία ἐστίν. γέγραπται γὰρ Ὁ δρα όμενο τοὺ οφοὺ ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ
αὐτῶν. Ἐγὼ φημὶ οὐ μέγα πρᾶγμα εἶναι ἐὰν ὁ θεὸς ὡς θεὸς δράξηται τοὺς σοφοὺς ἐν
τῇ πανουργίᾳ αὐτῶν, <ἀλλ'> ἐν Παύλῳ τῷ λέγοντι ἐν αρκὶ γὰρ ζῶντες οὐ κατὰ
άρκα τρατευόμεθα· τὰ γὰρ ὅπλα τῆ τρατεία ἡμῶν οὐ αρκικὰ ἀλλὰ δυνατὰ τῷ θεῷ
πρὸ καθαίρε ιν ὀχυρωμάτων· λογι μοὺ καθαιροῦντε καὶ πᾶν ὕψωμα ἐπαιρόμενον
κατὰ τῆ γνώ εω τοῦ θεοῦ. ἵνα δὲ τοῦτο σαφέστερον νοήσῃς, ἴδε μοι τὸν Παῦλον
ἐπιδημήσαντα ταῖς Ἀθήναις καὶ ζητοῦντα πρὸ τοὺ παρατυγχάνοντα ὥστε καί τινας
τῶν Ἐπικουρείων καὶ Στωικῶν φιλο όφων συμβα λεῖν αὐτῷ, τότε γὰρ τῇ χάριτι τοῦ
Χριστοῦ περιεδράσσετο αὐτῶν καὶ ἐδείκνυεν αὐτῶν τὰ σοφίσματα· ἐνταῦθα δὲ τοὺς
σοφοὺς ὠνομάσθαι νομίζω τοὺς σοφιστάς, ὅσοι σοφίσματα περιπεπλεγμένα
λέγουσιν οὐκ ἀλήθειαν δὲ διδάσκουσιν. καὶ πάλιν Κύριο γινώ κει τοὺ διαλογι μοὺ
τῶν σοφῶν ὅτι εἰ ὶ μάταιοι. Οὐ θαυμαστὸν ἐὰν ὁ Κύριος καθ' ἑαυτοῦ γινώσκει τοὺς
διαλογισμοὺς τῶν σοφῶν ὅτι εἰσὶ μάταιοι· ἀλλὰ θέλω ἐν ἐμοὶ γενόμενον τὸν Κύριον
γινώσκειν τοὺς διαλογισμοὺς τῶν σοφῶν ὅτι εἰσὶ μάταιοι. ἐὰν γὰρ γένηται ἐν ἐμοὶ
Χρι τό , δύναταί μοι παραστῆσαι πῶς οἱ διαλογισμοὶ τῶν τοῦ κόσμου σοφῶν εἰσὶ
μάταιοι καὶ πῶς λάμπει ἡ σοφία μόνη τοῦ θεοῦ νικῶσα καὶ καταπατοῦσα πᾶσαν
δοκοῦ σαν σοφίαν. 17 iii 21–23 [ὥστε μηδεὶς καυχάσθω ἐν ἀνθρώποις· πάντα γὰρ
ὑμῶν ἐστιν, εἴτε Παῦλος εἴτε Ἀπολλὼς εἴτε Κηφᾶς εἴτε κόσμος εἴτε ζωὴ εἴτε θάνατος
εἴτε ἐνεστῶτα εἴτε μέλλοντα· πάντα ὑμῶν ἐστιν, ὑμεῖς δὲ Χριστοῦ, Χριστὸς δὲ θεοῦ.]
[Ὠριγένους] Ὁ δυνάμενος ἀποτάξα θαι πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις καὶ ὅλος γενέσθαι ἄξιος
τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ καυχήσεως, οὗτος οὐκ ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ καυχᾶται. Πῶς δὲ ὁ θάνατος ἐμός
ἐστιν; ἵνα ἀποθάνω τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ· ἵνα εἴπω Εἰ καὶ υναπεθάνομεν, καὶ υζή ομεν. ὁ γὰρ
ἄλλος θάνατος καθ' ὃν ἡ ψυχὴ ἡ ἁμαρτά νου α αὐτὴ ἀποθανεῖται οὐκ ἔστιν ἐμός. καὶ
τὰ ἐνεστῶτα δὲ ἡμῶν ἐστιν· ὅτι συναγόμεθα ἐν τῷ ἐνεστῶτι αἰῶνι, ὅτι ἀκούομεν
γραφῶν ἱερῶν, ὅτι εὐχόμεθα. τὰ δὲ μέλλοντα· ὅταν γὰρ ἔλθῃ τὸ τέλειον, τότε τὸ ἐκ
μέρου καταρτηθή εται. καὶ οὐχ οἷόν τέ ἐστιν ἐπὶ τὰ μέλλοντα ἐλθεῖν ἐὰν μὴ πρῶτον
γένηταί μοι τὰ ἐνεστῶτα. πάντα ὑμῶν· θαυμάζεταί τις λόγος παρ' Ἕλλησιν
εἰρημένος τοιοῦτος· «Πάντα τοῦ σοφοῦ καὶ οὐδὲν τοῦ φαύλου·» ταῦτα δὲ ὁ λόγος
τοῦ θεοῦ πρῶτος ἐδίδαξεν ὅτι Πάντα τοῦ ἁγίου ἐστίν. τοῦ οὖν πιστοῦ, φησίν, ὅλος ὁ
κόσμος τῶν χρημάτων, τοῦ δὲ ἀπίστου οὐδὲ ὀβολός· ὡς γὰρ λῃστὴς ἔχει ἃ ἔχει ὁ
ἄπιστος· οὐ γὰρ εἰδὼς αὐτοῖς χρῆσθαι οὐδὲ τὸν κτίσαντα ταῦτα θεὸν οὐδὲ ἀκούων
τοῦ λέγοντος Ἐμὸν τὸ ἀργύριον καὶ ἐμὸν τὸ χρυ ίον, οὐχ ὡς αὐτοῦ ἐκεῖνα ἔχει. ἡμεῖς
δὲ ὁρῶμεν ὅτι πάντα ἡμῶν ἐστιν· καὶ ἔστι τοῦ <πιστοῦ> ὅλος ὁ κόσμος τῶν
χρημάτων τοῦ δὲ ἀπίστου οὐδὲ ὀβολός. 18 iν 1–5 [οὕτως ἡμᾶς λογιζέσθω ἄνθρωπος
ὡς ὑπηρέτας Χριστοῦ καὶ οἰκονό μους μυστηρίων θεοῦ. ὃ δὲ λοιπὸν ζητεῖτε ἐν τοῖς
οἰκονόμοις ἵνα πιστός τις εὑρεθῇ. ἐμοὶ δὲ εἰς ἐλάχιστόν ἐστιν ἵνα ὑφ' ὑμῶν
ἀνακριθῶ ἢ ὑπὸ ἀνθρω πίνης ἡμέρας· ἀλλ' οὐδὲ ἐμαυτὸν ἀνακρίνω· οὐδὲν γὰρ
ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐν τούτῳ δεδικαίωμαι, ὁ δὲ ἀνακρίνων με Κύριός ἐστιν.
ὥστε μὴ πρὸ καιροῦ τι κρίνετε, ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ ὁ κύριος, ὃς καὶ φωτίσει τὰ κρυπτὰ τοῦ
σκότους καὶ φανερώσει τὰς βουλὰς τῶν καρδιῶν, καὶ τότε ὁ ἔπαινος γενήσεται
ἑκάστῳ ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ.]
[Ὠριγένους] Ὁ μὴ διαβεβηκὼς τῷ λόγῳ περὶ τὴν
κατάληψιν τῶν ἐγκεκρυμμένων ἐν τῇ γραφῇ μυστηρίων δύναται μὲν ὑπηρέτης εἶναι
Χριστοῦ, οὐ δύναται δὲ οἰκονόμος εἶναι μυστηρίων θεοῦ· ὁ γὰρ οἰκονόμος ὢν ἔχει τὰ
οἰκονομούμενα καὶ οἶδεν τὰ μυ τήρια τοῦ θεοῦ. μή ποτε οὖν ὁ μὲν ὑπηρέτης Χριστοῦ
κατὰ τὴν κοινοτέ ραν νοεῖται διακονίαν προστάς, ὁ δὲ οἰκονόμος μυστηρίων θεοῦ
κατὰ τὴν διοίκησιν τὴν περὶ τὰ γνωσθέντα μυστήρια, ἵνα μὴ παρα<ρ>ρίπτῃ ταῦτα ὡς
ἔτυχεν μηδὲ ἀνεξετάστως αὐτὰ παραδιδῷ· ἀλλὰ προκαθάρας, προευτρεπίσας,
προαποστήσας τοῦ κόσμου τὸν μέλλοντα ἀκούειν μαθημάτων ὑπερκοσμίων, τότε
αὐτ<ὰ> λέγει. Ἡμεῖς, φησίν, ἐσμὲν ὑπηρέται Χριστοῦ· καὶ τὰ πλείονα μᾶλλον ὁ
ἀπόστολος τῇ ὑπηρεσίᾳ τοῦ Χριστοῦ διηκονεῖτο ἤπερ τῇ οἰκονομίᾳ τῶν μυστηρίων
pass_a_gloss: Rem early continues the open mid phrase: all things have been put together, or that pleasure is the end of goods, and the rest of the outside seeming wisdoms empty chatter; such a person is truly a fool and those dogmas are folly. Examining all Greek and barbarian philosophy you will say that wherever it disagrees with Christs teaching it is folly; for it is written he catches the wise in their craftiness. I say it is no great thing if God as God catches the wise in their craftiness, but rather in Paul who says living in flesh we do not wage war according to flesh; the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly but powerful with God for tearing down strongholds, tearing down reasonings and every height raised against the knowledge of God. To see this more clearly picture Paul arriving at Athens seeking opportunity so that some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers clash with him; then by Christs grace he was catching them and showing their sophisms. Here I think the wise named are the sophists who speak entangled sophisms and do not teach truth. And again the Lord knows the reasonings of the wise that they are futile. It is no wonder if the Lord by himself knows those reasonings are futile; but I want the Lord come to be in me knowing the wise reasonings are futile. For if Christ comes to be in me he can show me how the worlds wise reasonings are futile and how Gods wisdom alone shines conquering and trampling every seeming wisdom. Then 1 Cor 3:21-23: so let no one boast in humans; all things are yours whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or world or life or death or present or future; all are yours, you are Christs, Christ is Gods. Origen: the one able to renounce all humans and become wholly worthy of boasting in Christ does not boast in a human. How is death mine? That I may die to sin; that I may say if we died with him we will also live with him. The other death by which the sinning soul itself will die is not mine. Present things are ours too: we gather in the present age, hear holy scriptures, pray. Future things: when the perfect comes then what is in part will be done away. One cannot reach the future unless the present first becomes mine. All things yours: among Greeks a saying is admired that all things belong to the wise and nothing to the worthless; Gods word first taught that all things belong to the holy. Of the faithful then the whole world of goods, of the unfaithful not even an obol; the unfaithful holds what he holds as a robber, not knowing how to use them nor the God who made them nor hearing mine is the silver and mine the gold, so he does not hold them as his. We see that all things are ours; and of the faithful the whole world of goods, of the unfaithful not even an obol. Then 1 Cor 4:1-5 on reckoning us as Christs servants and stewards of Gods mysteries, seeking faithfulness in stewards, Paul little concerned to be examined by them or by a human day, not even examining himself though he knows nothing against himself yet is not justified thereby, the Lord examining him; so do not judge before the time until the Lord comes who will light the darks hidden things and reveal hearts plans, then each will have praise from God. Origen: one who has not crossed in the word to grasp mysteries hidden in scripture can be Christs servant but not steward of Gods mysteries; the steward has what is administered and knows Gods mysteries. Perhaps Christs servant is understood by the more common ministry, while steward of Gods mysteries by the management of known mysteries, so he does not toss them at random or hand them over unexamined, but after cleansing, preparing, and drawing the hearer away from the world for supra-worldly lessons, then he speaks. We are Christs servants, he says; and the Apostle more often served Christs service than the stewardship of Gods mysteries
pass_b_english: all things have been put together—or that pleasure is the end of goods—and saying the rest of what the outside, seeming wisdom chatters and prates. For such a person is truly a fool, and those doctrines are folly. And when you examine all Greek and barbarian philosophy simply, you will say that wherever it disagrees with Christ’s teaching it is folly. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness.”

I say it is no great thing if God, as God, catches the wise in their craftiness—but rather in Paul, who says, “For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly but powerful with God for the tearing down of strongholds, tearing down reasonings and every height raised against the knowledge of God.” To understand this more clearly, picture Paul arriving in Athens and seeking opportunity among those he meets, so that some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers even clash with him; then by Christ’s grace he was catching hold of them and exposing their sophisms. Here I take “the wise” to mean the sophists—whoever spins entangled sophisms and does not teach truth.

And again: “The Lord knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are futile.” It is no wonder if the Lord, by himself, knows that the reasonings of the wise are futile. But I want the Lord, come to be in me, to know that the reasonings of the wise are futile. For if Christ comes to be in me, he can set beside me how the reasonings of this world’s wise are futile, and how God’s wisdom alone shines, conquering and trampling every seeming wisdom.

1 Cor. 3:21–23: “So let no one boast in human beings. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future—all are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.” Origen says: The one who can renounce all human beings and become wholly worthy of the boast that is in Christ does not boast in a human being. How, then, is death mine? So that I may die to sin; so that I may say, “If we died with him, we will also live with him.” For the other death—by which the sinning soul itself will die—is not mine. Present things too are ours: that we gather in the present age, hear the holy Scriptures, pray. And the future: when the perfect comes, then what is in part will be done away. And it is not possible to come to the future unless the present first becomes mine.

“All things are yours.” Among the Greeks a saying of this sort is admired: “All things belong to the wise, and nothing to the worthless.” But the word of God first taught that all things belong to the holy. Of the faithful, then, he says, the whole world of goods; of the unfaithful, not even an obol. For the unfaithful holds what he holds as a robber: not knowing how to use these things, nor knowing the God who made them, nor hearing the one who says, “Mine is the silver and mine the gold,” he does not hold them as his own. But we see that all things are ours; and of the faithful the whole world of goods, of the unfaithful not even an obol.

1 Cor. 4:1–5: “This is how one should regard us: as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required in stewards that one be found faithful. But with me it is a very small thing that I should be examined by you or by a human day. I do not even examine myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby justified. It is the Lord who examines me. So do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will disclose the purposes of the hearts. Then each one will receive his praise from God.”

Origen says: The one who has not crossed over in the word to the grasp of the mysteries hidden in Scripture can be a servant of Christ, but cannot be a steward of God’s mysteries. For the steward has what is administered and knows the mysteries of God. Perhaps, then, the servant of Christ is understood according to the more common ministry, while the steward of God’s mysteries is understood according to the management that concerns the mysteries once known—so that he does not toss them about at random, nor hand them over unexamined, but first cleanses, prepares, and draws away from the world the one who is about to hear supra-worldly lessons, and only then speaks them.
“We,” he says, “are servants of Christ.” And for the most part the Apostle served the service of Christ more than the stewardship of the mysteries
